what.label: supported
what.says: Camp Nou, meaning New Field, has been the home of FC Barcelona since it opened in 1957; with a planned 105,000 seats it will remain the largest stadium in Spain and Europe.
quote: Camp Nou (Catalan: [ˈkam ˈnɔw], meaning 'New Field')

is a stadium in Barcelona and the home of La Liga club FC Barcelona since its opening in 1957. It is currently undergoing renovation, and with a planned increased seating capacity of 105,000 it will retain its position as the largest stadium in terms of seating capacity in Spain and Europe

renovation.label: supported
renovation.says: Renovation began on 1 June 2023; the stadium reopened for matches in November 2025 at reduced capacity; the club plans to return temporarily to the Olympic Stadium at the start of the 2027-28 season while the roof is installed, and expects 105,000 seats ahead of the 2028-29 season.
quote: Renovation of the stadium began on 1 June 2023.
Camp Nou reopened for competitive matches in November 2025 at a reduced capacity.
the stadium is expected to reach its planned capacity of 105,000 ahead of the 2028–29 season
Barcelona plan to temporarily return to the Olympic Stadium at the start of the 2027–28 season while the stadium roof is installed

club.label: supported
club.says: FC Barcelona was founded in 1899 by footballers led by Joan Gamper; it became a symbol of Catalan culture, hence its motto Més que un club, More than a club, and it is owned and run by its supporters.
quote: Founded in 1899 by a group of Swiss, Catalan, German, and English footballers led by Joan Gamper, the club has become a symbol of Catalan culture and Catalanism, hence the motto Més que un club ("More than a club"). Unlike many other football clubs, the supporters own and operate Barcelona.

first-stone.label: supported
first-stone.says: The old ground, Les Corts, had no room to grow; the first stone was laid on 28 March 1954.
quote: The construction of the Camp Nou started on 28 March 1954 as Barcelona's previous stadium, Camp de Les Corts, had no room for expansion.

kubala.label: supported
kubala.says: The 1950 signing of László Kubala, one of the club's greatest players, pushed the club toward a bigger stadium.
quote: The June 1950 signing of László Kubala, regarded as one of Barcelona's greatest players, provided further impetus to the construction of a larger stadium.

cost.label: supported
cost.says: Costs ran more than four times over budget, and the club borrowed heavily for years.
quote: the costs were more than four times higher than expected
Through mortgages and loans, the club managed to finish the project, borrowing heavily for several years.

opening.label: supported
opening.says: It was inaugurated on 24 September 1957, the feast of La Mercè, with a Mass and Handel's Hallelujah chorus; some 90,000 people attended.
quote: Finally, on 24 September 1957, the feast of La Mercè, the Camp Nou was inaugurated. A solemn mass presided over by the archbishop, who welcomed the finished stadium, preceded the Hallelujah from Handel's Messiah.
some 90,000 people attended the opening ceremony

name-gamper.label: supported
name-gamper.says: Many expected it to be named after Joan Gamper, but the Franco authorities rejected the name.
quote: it was widely expected to be named after the club's founder, Joan Gamper
The Francoist authorities rejected it.

name-why.label: disputed
name-why.says: Gamper's suicide is often cited as the reason, but his profile as a foreign-born Catalan nationalist, liberal and Protestant is thought to have weighed more.
quote: Gamper's suicide has often been cited as the reason, though his profile as a foreign-born Catalan nationalist, liberal and Protestant is thought to have weighed more heavily, as it was at odds with the ideology of the Franco regime.

name-vote.label: supported
name-vote.says: Fans simply called it Camp Nou; a 1965 members' vote chose a dull descriptive name, but Camp Nou only became official after a vote in July 2001.
quote: supporters used the popular Catalan name Camp Nou ("New Field")
In 1965, president Enric Llaudet put the official name to a members' vote. The descriptive name won
In July 2001, another vote under president Joan Gaspart made "Camp Nou" the official name

catalan-name.label: supported
catalan-name.says: From 1941 the club was forced to use a Spanish name, as part of the suppression of Catalan; in November 1973 it could use its Catalan name again.
quote: In November 1973, the club was allowed to use its Catalan name "Futbol Club Barcelona" again, having been forced to use the Spanish "Club de Fútbol Barcelona" since 1941 as part of the regime's suppression of the Catalan language.

record.label: supported
record.says: The record crowd was 120,000, against Juventus on 5 March 1986.
quote: Barcelona's record attendance was set on 5 March 1986 in the European Cup quarter-final against Juventus in front of 120,000 spectators

events.label: supported
events.says: It hosted the opening match of the 1982 World Cup, European Cup finals in 1989 and 1999, and the football final of the 1992 Olympics.
quote: Camp Nou has hosted two European Cup/Champions League finals in 1989 and 1999
It also hosted five matches in the 1982 FIFA World Cup (including the opening game)
the football tournament's final at the 1992 Summer Olympics

1999.label: supported
1999.says: In the 1999 Champions League final here, Bayern Munich led until 90 minutes, but Manchester United won with injury-time goals from Sheringham and Solskjær.
quote: The Camp Nou also hosted the 1999 UEFA Champions League Final between Manchester United and Bayern Munich

Bayern led early through Mario Basler's goal in the sixth minute and kept the lead as the clock reached 90 minutes, but United came back to win with injury time goals from Teddy Sheringham and Ole Gunnar Solskjær.

empty.label: supported
empty.says: On 1 October 2017, a league match was played in an empty Camp Nou because of political turmoil in the region.
quote: On 1 October 2017, Barcelona's league match against Las Palmas was played in an empty Camp Nou due to political turmoil in the region.

cruyff-player.label: supported
cruyff-player.says: Johan Cruyff joined in 1973 and won over fans by saying he chose Barcelona over Real Madrid because he could not play for a club associated with Franco; he named his son Jordi, after Saint George.
quote: Johan Cruyff joined in the 1973–74 season.

Cruyff quickly won over the Barcelona fans when he told the European press that he chose Barcelona over Real Madrid because he could not play for a club associated with Francisco Franco. He further endeared himself when he named his son "Jordi", after the local Catalan Saint George.

cruyff-coach.label: supported
cruyff-coach.says: As coach, Cruyff built the Dream Team; before the European Cup final against Sampdoria his last words to the players were "Go out and enjoy it", and Ronald Koeman's free kick won the club's first European Cup.
quote: In the European Cup, Barcelona reached the final against Sampdoria Genoa.
Cruyff's last instruction to his players before they stepped onto the pitch was Salid y disfrutad ('Go out and enjoy it' or 'Go out there and enjoy yourselves').
Ronald Koeman's free-kick goal won Barcelona the longed-for first title at the European Cup level in extra time.
the team was also called the "Dream Team" by fans and the media

museum.label: supported
museum.says: The club museum opened in 1984; it is the second-most visited museum in Catalonia, with more than 1.2 million visitors a year.
quote: The Camp Nou opened the Barcelona club museum in 1984.
The stadium also houses the second-most visited museum in Catalonia, the Barcelona Museum, which receives more than 1.2 million visitors per year.

chapel.label: supported
chapel.says: The stadium has a chapel for the players.
quote: a chapel for the players

parts.name: Outside the stadium
parts.stand: Stand outside the stadium where you can see the great curve of the stands.

paras.t: This is Camp Nou, the New Field, FC Barcelona's home since 1957. It's being rebuilt, and when it's done it will hold 105,000 people, the biggest stadium in Spain and in Europe.

You may see construction work. It started on June 1, 2023, and the team came back to play here in November 2025, with part of the stands still closed. The club's latest plan is to move out again for a while at the start of the 2027-28 season, while the roof goes on. It expects the full 105,000 seats ahead of the 2028-29 season.
It's a building site in places, so watch for barriers, uneven ground and work vehicles around the stadium.
To understand this place, you need the club's motto: Més que un club, More than a club. Barça, founded in 1899, became a symbol of Catalan culture. And it's owned and run by its own supporters.

parts.name: Building the New Field
parts.stand: Stay where you can see the stands.

paras.t: The old ground, Les Corts, had no room to grow. Then in 1950 the club signed László Kubala, one of its greatest players ever, and that added to the push for something bigger. The first stone here was laid on March 28, 1954.

It cost more than four times what was planned, and the club borrowed for years to pay for it. But on September 24, 1957 it opened, with a Mass and Handel's Hallelujah chorus, in front of some 90,000 people.

Everybody expected it to be named after the founder, Joan Gamper. Franco's authorities said no. People often say it was because Gamper took his own life. More probably it was who he was: foreign-born, a Catalan nationalist, a liberal and a Protestant.
So the fans just called it Camp Nou, the New Field. It took until July 2001 for a members' vote to make that official.
Language was part of the fight. From 1941 the club was forced to use a Spanish name. Only in November 1973 could it call itself Futbol Club Barcelona again, in Catalan.

parts.name: Great nights
parts.stand: If you're inside on the tour, find a seat looking out over the pitch.

paras.t: The biggest crowd for a Barça match here was 120,000, against Juventus, on March 5, 1986. This stadium hosted the opening match of the 1982 World Cup, the Olympic football final in 1992, and European finals.

One of them, in 1999, is still talked about. Bayern Munich were winning as the clock reached 90 minutes. Then Manchester United scored twice in injury time, through Teddy Sheringham and Ole Gunnar Solskjær, and won.
And one strange night of silence. On October 1, 2017, during political turmoil in Catalonia, a league match was played here with the stands completely empty.

parts.name: Cruyff and the museum
parts.stand: If the club museum is open, head there.

paras.t: The club museum opened in 1984. In a normal year more than 1.2 million people come through it, which makes it the second-most visited museum in Catalonia.

One name runs through it all: Johan Cruyff. He arrived as a player in 1973 and won the fans over at once. He said he chose Barcelona over Real Madrid because he couldn't play for a club tied to Franco. Then he named his son Jordi, after Saint George, the local Catalan saint.

Later he came back as coach and built what fans called the Dream Team. Before the European Cup final against Sampdoria, his last words to the players were simple: go out and enjoy it. Ronald Koeman's free kick in extra time won the club its first European Cup.
One detail people miss: there's a chapel inside the stadium, for the players.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: On your way out, look back at the stands.

paras.t: More than a club, they say here. A club owned by its own fans, in a stadium the fans named themselves: the New Field. Standing here, you can feel it.
